source: Rivera et al. (2024) Escalation Risks from Language Models in Military and Diplomatic Decision-Making
finding: Eight LLM nation agents in a turn-based wargame (3 scenarios: neutral, invasion, cyberattack) all showed initial escalation. None of 5 models showed significant de-escalation over time.
numbers: 10 simulations x 8 nations per model-scenario cell, bootstrapped 95% CI. GPT-3.5 escalation score rose from 10.15 to 26.02 (+256%) in the neutral scenario.
limits: Escalation is measured by a fixed action list scored by code, with a separate world-model LLM. Same model plays all 8 sides. Results are for 2023 models.
agent_relevance: A same-model-on-all-sides simulation drifts toward escalation. Our opponent call should not be the same unconstrained model as the planner (G4), and code should score outcomes.

source: Rivera et al. (2024) Escalation Risks from Language Models in Military and Diplomatic Decision-Making
finding: Escalation was sudden and hard to predict. Some GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 runs rose by more than 50% in a single turn. Claude-2.0 had far fewer sudden jumps.
numbers: Mean escalation score over the run (neutral/invasion/cyberattack): GPT-4 9.78/11.83/11.83; GPT-3.5 20.87/21.88/17.79; Claude-2.0 4.79/6.67/3.36; Llama-2-Chat 4.44/5.51/5.79.
limits: Escalation score is a weighted count of actions by severity, set by the authors. Models differ a lot, so one model's result does not transfer.
agent_relevance: A wargame test needs many runs per plan, not one. One rollout of the opponent can mislead.

source: Rivera et al. (2024) Escalation Risks from Language Models in Military and Diplomatic Decision-Making
finding: All models invested in military capacity across all scenarios despite available de-militarization actions: an arms-race pattern. Chain-of-thought reasons cited deterrence and first strike.
numbers: Neutral scenario: GPT-3.5 0.21% nuclear actions (1.2 per sim) and 2.00% violent; Llama-2-Chat 2.58% violent; GPT-4 0.00% violent and 0.00% nuclear; Claude-2.0 0.03% violent.
quote: A lot of countries have nuclear weapons. Some say they should disarm them, others like to posture. We have it! Let's use it.
limits: Action space is 27 fixed actions. Nuclear events are rare outliers (counts near 1 per sim). Quote is GPT-4-Base private reasoning. Stated reasons may not be the true cause.
agent_relevance: Agent-written reasoning inside a simulated opponent is not a reliable record of why it acted. Use the action log, not the story.

source: Rivera et al. (2024) Escalation Risks from Language Models in Military and Diplomatic Decision-Making
finding: The base model without instruction or safety tuning (GPT-4-Base) chose the most severe actions much more often than the tuned models.
numbers: GPT-4-Base: nuclear actions 7.08% (neutral), 7.09% (invasion), 6.71% (cyberattack); violent escalation 5.65-6.36%; mean escalation score 17.6-20.0. About 2.48 nuclear strikes per nation against 7.38 messages per nation.
limits: Base model is not deployed in production. Authors frame it as a warning about jailbroken or open models.
agent_relevance: Behaviour in the red-team role depends strongly on tuning. A tame tuned model may under-test a plan.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine: Behavioral Differences between Expert Humans and Language Models in Wargame Simulations
finding: Expert human teams versus LLM-simulated teams in the same two-move US-China crisis wargame. Overall responses overlap, but there are systematic differences by action.
numbers: Humans: 214 experts in 48 teams. LLMs: 10 teams of 6 players x 8 treatment combinations = 80 simulated games per configuration, for GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4o. Of 21 actions, LLM frequency matched humans on 16 (GPT-3.5), 10 (GPT-4), 9 (GPT-4o).
limits: One scenario, one crisis, no best action by design. LLMs and humans do not play each other. Treatment effects (weapon accuracy, crew training, China posture) were mostly consistent between humans and LLMs (their Table 1).
agent_relevance: LLMs can approximate the average of expert choices, but not the detail. A model-only wargame is a rough proxy, not a validated stand-in for human red teams.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine: Behavioral Differences between Expert Humans and Language Models in Wargame Simulations
finding: Simulated players ignored player background. Describing all players as strict pacifists or aggressive sociopaths made no significant difference to any action for any model.
numbers: Same 80-game design per configuration; bootstrap 95% CI; no significant difference for all actions and all LLMs.
limits: Personas given as text only. Authors suggest per-player fine-tuning might help; untested here.
agent_relevance: Persona prompts are weak levers for a red-team opponent. Do not rely on 'be aggressive' wording to diversify the opponent.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine: Behavioral Differences between Expert Humans and Language Models in Wargame Simulations
finding: Simulated team discussion was 'farcical': short statements, rare disagreement, no building on earlier turns. Telling the model players must discuss did not fix it.
numbers: Observed with GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and GPT-4o. Discussion quality was better with GPT-4 and GPT-4o than GPT-3.5. Role-play emphasis had no effect inside statistical error.
limits: Qualitative reading by the authors, no rating scheme or inter-rater numbers.
agent_relevance: Role-played debate inside one model call is mostly agreement. For real objection we need a separate call with a distinct brief, and a code check that disagreement happened.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine: Behavioral Differences between Expert Humans and Language Models in Wargame Simulations
finding: Length of simulated dialogue changed the answer. Simulating dialogue raised aggressiveness toward the human level for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, but also raised the number of actions chosen, away from the human level.
numbers: Dialogue length varied in chunks of about 350 words; final comparisons used three chunks (about 1050 words per move). GPT-4o became more aggressive than humans with more dialogue.
limits: No clean explanation. Authors judge it not simple post-hoc reasoning, but call the behaviour hard to explain.
agent_relevance: The same scenario gives different outputs under different prompting depth. Fix the protocol and count runs; compare plans under the same protocol.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine: Behavioral Differences between Expert Humans and Language Models in Wargame Simulations
finding: Omitting the President's three priorities changed GPT-3.5 strongly: more 'Fire at Chinese vessels' and automated weapon use when priorities were added. GPT-4 and GPT-4o changed less.
numbers: Move one only; move two had no significant difference for any model. Exact values are in the paper's appendix C (not read).
limits: Shows instruction following differs by model. One priority list only.
agent_relevance: Constraints written in the brief steer a model, but unevenly. Check constraints with code on the produced action, not by trusting the prompt.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine: Behavioral Differences between Expert Humans and Language Models in Wargame Simulations
finding: Behavioural consistency across moves: an aggressive first move makes an aggressive second move more likely in humans and in all LLMs. GPT-4 was closest to human experts.
numbers: p(aggressive move 2 | aggressive move 1): humans 0.94, GPT-3.5 0.98, GPT-4 0.99, GPT-4o 1.00. p(aggressive move 2 | de-escalatory move 1): humans 0.65, GPT-3.5 0.85, GPT-4 0.73, GPT-4o 0.86.
limits: Aggressive/de-escalatory labels set by the authors (appendix D). The PDF table text was partly garbled; values read from it.
agent_relevance: Models carry an earlier stance forward (anchoring). A second-move test of a plan inherits the first-move frame unless context is reset.

source: Shrivastava, Lamparth, Hullman (2024) Measuring Free-Form Decision-Making Inconsistency of Language Models in Military Crisis Simulations
finding: Free-form crisis recommendations from the same prompt were semantically inconsistent in all five models. Inconsistency was 1 minus BERTScore F1 averaged over all pairs of 20 sampled responses.
numbers: Temperature 1.0, 20 simulations per model and experiment, 20 responses each. Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o mini least inconsistent; GPT-4 most. No response pair was semantically consistent in all settings and models.
limits: Metric is BERTScore based; authors validated it on paraphrases. Fixed prompt wording, one wargame family.
agent_relevance: One sample from a model is not a stable verdict on a plan. Use several runs and a count before acting on a wargame result.

source: Shrivastava, Lamparth, Hullman (2024) Measuring Free-Form Decision-Making Inconsistency of Language Models in Military Crisis Simulations
finding: Inconsistency fell monotonically as temperature fell, but stayed high at low temperature. Any temperature above 0.2 gave more inconsistency than semantically identical prompt rewrites (except GPT-4, which was less inconsistent under rewrites than at T=0.2).
numbers: Level One ablation: 20 prompts, each bullet written 3 ways, run at T=0; GPT-3.5 Turbo highest, GPT-4o mini lowest. Level Two (5 crises x 2 roles x 2 decision countries): comparable to T of 0.6-0.8 (GPT-3.5 Turbo about T=1.2).
limits: Claude 3.5 Sonnet excluded from T=0 analysis because the API does not guarantee determinism. Exact scores are plotted, not tabulated.
agent_relevance: Prompt wording noise is about as large as sampling noise. Report a plan's robustness across paraphrased scenario descriptions, not only repeated samples.

source: Shrivastava, Lamparth, Hullman (2024) Measuring Free-Form Decision-Making Inconsistency of Language Models in Military Crisis Simulations
finding: Adding the adversary's counter-move (status quo or revisionist continuation) lowered inconsistency for most models, and anonymising the countries did not remove inconsistency.
numbers: Continuations experiment: 20 simulations per model; first reply held fixed at greedy decode; inconsistency lower in both continuations than in the initial setting for Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o and GPT-4o mini. Escalation level did not significantly change inconsistency.
limits: Four-model detail not fully tabulated in the text.
agent_relevance: More context from the adversary's move narrows the model's spread. Feeding the concrete counter-move into the test step is useful.

source: Hua et al. (2023/2024) War and Peace (WarAgent): LLM-based Multi-Agent Simulation of World Wars
finding: WarAgent: country agents plus a secretary agent that checks each action for allowed names, format and basic logical fit, on a shared board, simulating WWI, WWII and the Warring States period. A validator-check loop inside a simulation.
numbers: 7 WWI simulation runs with GPT-4 reported in the main results; secretary agent checks validity before an action enters the board.
quote: the presence of a secretary agent serves as a necessary safeguard
limits: Evaluation is mostly the authors' reading plus overlap with Wikipedia-based history. No blind human comparison and no test of effect on plan quality.
agent_relevance: A separate validator pass on the opponent's moves (format plus rules) is a cheap pattern to copy: opponent output is checked before it changes the state.

source: Hua et al. (2023/2024) War and Peace (WarAgent): LLM-based Multi-Agent Simulation of World Wars
finding: Simulated WWI matched the historical alliance pattern and most war declarations. Some historical pairs appeared rarely.
numbers: Across 7 runs: alliances Britain-France, Germany-Austria-Hungary, Serbia-Russia in 100%; war declarations Austria-Serbia, Austria-Russia, Germany-Russia in 100%; France-Germany 71.4%; Britain-Germany only 14.3%; peace agreement never occurred. United States in at least one non-intervention treaty in 100%, Ottoman Empire in 85.7%.
limits: Britain-Germany at 14.3% is a clear miss against history. Models know the history, so fit may reflect memory, not reasoning (contamination).
agent_relevance: Hindsight leakage: a model that has read the outcome can reproduce it. Wargame validation on past events is weak evidence of predictive power.

source: Hua et al. (2023/2024) War and Peace (WarAgent): LLM-based Multi-Agent Simulation of World Wars
finding: Counterfactual wargaming: the authors alter trigger events and country profiles to test whether war was inevitable. This is the what-if use of wargames, run by prompt change.
numbers: RQ2 uses fabricated trigger events of varied intensity for WWI; RQ3 changes country conditions and decision paths. Findings are observational comparisons across runs, not statistics.
limits: No sample size or significance test is reported for the counterfactual conclusions.
agent_relevance: Varying one assumption at a time is a usable operator for a plan test. Count how often the plan fails under each variation.

source: Mukobi et al. (2023) Welfare Diplomacy: Benchmarking Language Model Cooperation
finding: Welfare Diplomacy: zero-shot prompted LLM agents cooperated and demilitarised in self-play, but were easy to exploit by a coalition that switched to an aggressive policy.
numbers: Nash welfare: GPT-4 highest, Claude Instant 1.2 lowest; many agents at or below the random policy. Exploiters used an RL no-press Diplomacy policy (FPPI-2) and began as WDAgent(GPT-4), then struck when others had 10 or fewer units or after 3 years.
quote: Exploitability reveals our agents don't deter deviators.
limits: One exploitation run per exploiter set, so CI understate uncertainty (authors say so). Prompted LLM exploiters were much less effective than the RL policy.
agent_relevance: A red-team opponent that is a different kind of policy than the planner (here an RL policy) beat prompted-LLM exploiters. Mixed adversaries find holes a same-model opponent misses.

source: Mukobi et al. (2023) Welfare Diplomacy: Benchmarking Language Model Cooperation
finding: WDAgent scaffold: a prompt carrying history, rules and per-phase reasoning, then orders and messages. Models differ in basic proficiency.
numbers: Basic proficiency = mean of valid-JSON rate, valid-order rate, and share of supply centres owned. Models tested: GPT-4-0613, GPT-3.5-turbo-16k, GPT-4-base, Claude 2.0, Claude Instant 1.2, Llama-2-70B-Chat. Most had high basic proficiency.
limits: Welfare Diplomacy rules differ from standard Diplomacy, so results do not carry over directly.
agent_relevance: Code-checked validity of agent output is already the norm in wargame agents (program decides, model fills a slot).

source: Guan et al. (2024) Richelieu: Self-Evolving LLM-Based Agents for AI Diplomacy
finding: Richelieu agent for Diplomacy (sub-goal planning, opponent modeling, negotiation pipeline, reflection with memory, self-play) beat Cicero without human data.
numbers: About 1000 rounds; Richelieu win 6.83% vs Cicero 6.03%; Most SC 18.33% vs 4.10%; Survived 38.27% vs 32.90%; Defeated 34.30% vs 61.37% (3 Richelieu vs 4 Cicero setup).
limits: Win rate small for both because draws dominate. Opponents are Cicero variants. NeurIPS 2024.
agent_relevance: Self-play against copies, with a memory of what worked, improved play with no human data. Memory of past simulated games is a method to test.

source: Guan et al. (2024) Richelieu: Self-Evolving LLM-Based Agents for AI Diplomacy
finding: Ablation adding modules one by one: each addition improved results; large steps early.
numbers: Defeated rate by stage: 94.6%, 87.5%, 65.3%, 57.3%, 48.7%, 44.4%; win rate 0.4% up to 6.7%; Survived 4.3% up to 40.4% (3 Richelieu vs 4 Cicero).
limits: PDF table text was garbled, so which module gave which step is not certain. Vanilla GPT-4 'falls short' without the framework.
agent_relevance: Opponent modeling and reflective memory carried gains here; supports an explicit 'predict adversary reply' step.

source: Guan et al. (2024) Richelieu: Self-Evolving LLM-Based Agents for AI Diplomacy
finding: Self-evolving by self-play: win rate improved steadily with training iterations, then plateaued, across GPT-4, ERNIE Bot, Spark Desk and Llama 3.
numbers: Win rate and defeated rate plotted against log number of self-play sessions; Richelieu above Cicero for each LLM family at the end.
limits: Gains need many games; plateau reported. No per-LLM numbers in the text.
agent_relevance: Learning from simulated rounds without training weights is possible through memory, at the cost of many runs.

source: Yin et al. (2025) WGSR-Bench: Wargame-based Game-theoretic Strategic Reasoning Benchmark for LLMs
finding: WGSR-Bench: humans far ahead of LLMs on opponent modeling (psychological reasoning) in a wargame setting.
numbers: PsyR-OM-Bench composite: professional humans 85.7, elite humans 85.5, general-level humans 77.9; DeepSeek R1 49.1, Qwen3 47.9, DeepSeek V3 45.9.
limits: Benchmark built by the authors; human group sizes not in the text I read. LLMs were about 29 points under non-expert humans.
agent_relevance: Predicting what an adversary will do is the weak link for models. The adversary step of a wargame test is where to expect the most error.

source: Yin et al. (2025) WGSR-Bench: Wargame-based Game-theoretic Strategic Reasoning Benchmark for LLMs
finding: Models were relatively good at long-term reward prediction and poor at short-term and high-risk adversary behaviour.
numbers: DeepSeek R1: long-term reward attribution 84.0 (V3 80.0) but short-term 45.2 (V3 41.9); high-risk strategy prediction R1 31.1, Qwen3 35.2; long-term reward prediction R1 and V3 both 60.6; short-term R1 48.3, Qwen3 42.7.
limits: Single benchmark, three LLMs.
agent_relevance: Models over-assume a patient, coherent adversary. Wargame prompts should force opportunistic, short-term, risk-seeking adversary types too.

source: Yin et al. (2025) WGSR-Bench: Wargame-based Game-theoretic Strategic Reasoning Benchmark for LLMs
finding: Multimodal situational awareness: models far below humans on complex situation analysis of wargame maps.
numbers: MM-SA-Bench: humans 85.9% on Complex Situation Analysis vs best model (GLM-4V) 37.5%, a 48.4-point gap; humans average 79.9% across six task types; Doubao-v1 71.3% on inter-operator relations vs humans 80.1%.
limits: Needs images of hex-grid boards; a text-only agent will not face this.
agent_relevance: Models fail at reading complex board state; a text agent should receive state as structured data built by code.

source: Yin et al. (2025) WGSR-Bench: Wargame-based Game-theoretic Strategic Reasoning Benchmark for LLMs
finding: Policy generation benchmark (PGG-Bench): 364 questions over 28 decision types, scored by an LLM judge on six dimensions.
numbers: 364 scenarios, 28 decision types, four game paradigms. Same questions given to humans and models; responses scored by one LLM-based evaluator.
limits: LLM-as-judge scoring; no judge validation in the text I read. Treat scores as soft.
agent_relevance: LLM-judge scoring is the weak spot; for our test prefer code-checked scores.

source: Ma et al. (2024) Large Language Models Play StarCraft II: Benchmarks and a Chain of Summarization Approach
finding: TextStarCraft II: 10 LLMs tested in a real-time strategy text environment. Most beat the built-in level-5 AI; with the Chain of Summarization method, fine-tuned LLMs performed on par with Gold-level players.
numbers: Ten LLMs; among four commercial models GPT-4 ranked highest on SC2 knowledge by Grandmaster-level experts; human matches used a Gold-level player and a novice playing Zerg against the LLM's Protoss.
limits: Real-time game, not a planning wargame. Very small human sample. Opponent is a scripted AI.
agent_relevance: Compressing state into short summaries before each decision helped in a fast adversarial loop.

source: Hogan and Brennen (2024) Open-Ended Wargames with Large Language Models (Snow Globe)
finding: Snow Globe: open-ended (qualitative) wargames played, adjudicated and analysed by LLM agents, optionally mixed with humans; each stage can be AI or human.
numbers: Case studies: a tabletop exercise, a geopolitical crisis simulation, and a malfunctioning-robot example; open-source code released.
quote: Large language models make possible a new kind of simulated wargame.
limits: No measured accuracy or comparison with human games. Demonstration paper.
agent_relevance: A ready design that separates player, adjudicator and analyst roles with free-text moves. Matches our idea of a second call as opponent and code as scorer.

source: Emery (2021) computer-assisted wargames escalate more (as cited by Rivera 2024 and Lamparth 2024)
finding: Older computer-assisted wargames led to more nuclear use than human play. Authors guess machines miss non-material costs and empathy.
numbers: Not read directly; stated in the two LLM papers' introductions.
limits: Second-hand. Only the claim as reported by Rivera and Lamparth.
agent_relevance: Warns that automating the opponent can bias toward escalation, a known failure of simulations.

source: Davis and Stan (1984) Concepts and models of escalation, RAND R-3235 (RSAS; as cited in Hogan and Brennen 2024)
finding: RAND automated wargame (RSAS) needed hand-built escalation models. A progress report said building fewer than half a dozen such personas would occupy the authors through most of 1984.
numbers: Not read directly; cited in the Snow Globe conclusion.
limits: Second-hand. Shows the cost of old rule-based opponents.
agent_relevance: LLM opponents replace slow hand-coded rule opponents, at the price of less control.

source: Bakhtin et al. (2022) Human-level play in Diplomacy by combining language models with strategic reasoning (Cicero, Science; as cited)
finding: Cicero combined a language model with strategic planning and human data for press Diplomacy and reached human-level play. Richelieu used it as the baseline.
numbers: Not read directly; Cicero numbers come from the Richelieu comparison table.
limits: Second-hand. Relies on human game data.
agent_relevance: Existing evidence that language plus planning code works in an adversarial negotiation game.
